findings.issue_text: **`packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:93-97`** — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (see `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:13-29`) returns the *entire* zod `safeParse` result object (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed token. Google's `refreshAccessToken` does:

This persists `{ success: true, data: {...} }` as the credential's `key` — for **every** Google Calendar user, on **every** token refresh, regardless of whether the new sync feature is enabled. The next time this credential is loaded, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (constructor, `CalendarService.ts:74`) will fail because the shape no longer matches, breaking the user's calendar until they reconnect. This is a mainline regression, not an opt-in one. Fix: use `key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data`, or have the helper return `.data` (see office365's usage, which correctly destructures `.success`/`.data` — the two call sites disagree on the function's contract, which is itself the root cause).

**`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96`** — `prisma.credential.update(...)` is called but `prisma` is never imported in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`). This will fail TypeScript compilation / throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime, breaking the entire Salesforce integration (event creation, contact sync, everything that instantiates `SalesforceCalendarService`, since `getClient` runs in the constructor).

**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:5-16` + `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:176-192`** — When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw, unparsed `fetch` `Response` object. Hubspot's caller assumes it's already a deserialized `HubspotToken`:

**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:22-49`** — Authorization bug: for team installs, the function only checks that the requesting user is an *accepted member* of the team (`members: { some: { userId, accepted: true } }`) and then creates the credential and `return`s — the `throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam` check is only reached on the *non-team* branch (where `state?.teamId` is always falsy at that point, since the team branch already returned). Any regular team member — not just team admins/owners — can therefore install/link OAuth app credentials on behalf of the whole team. Given the helper's name and the fact it exists specifically to gate this kind of action, this looks like an inverted/misplaced check rather than intentional design. Fix: call `throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam({ teamId: state.teamId, userId })` inside the `if (state?.teamId)` branch instead of the member-only lookup, and drop the now-dead `state?.teamId ?? null` call after it.

**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5-11`** — `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed property keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. `ZodString#toString()` isn't overridden, so both evaluate to the same literal string `"[object Object]"`, and the second silently clobbers the first. The comments ("assume any property with a number is the expiry", "allow other properties") describe intent that this code does not implement — the resulting schema only requires `access_token: z.string()` and passively allows one meaningless extra key. This means the sync-enabled path performs essentially no validation of the expiry field, so a malformed sync-endpoint response won't be caught here.

**`refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-14`** — the outbound `fetch` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no `response.ok` check, no timeout, and sends no authentication/shared secret, asymmetric with the inbound webhook (`app-credential.ts`) which does verify a shared secret. A misbehaving or unreachable sync endpoint will have its (possibly error-page) body treated as a valid token response with no error surfaced beyond a generic parse failure downstream, and there's no way for the receiving endpoint to authenticate that the request truly came from Cal.com.

**`salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:76-98`** — the refresh_token exchange now runs unconditionally on *every* `getClient` call (i.e., every time `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed), with no expiry check, unlike every other provider touched in this PR (which all gate refresh behind `isExpired`/`isTokenValid`). Refreshing on every request risks provider-side rate limiting and, since many OAuth providers rotate/invalidate the previous access token on refresh, concurrent requests could race each other. It also doesn't use `refreshOAuthTokens`, so Salesforce silently doesn't participate in the new credential-sync feature the PR is meant to deliver. Additionally, `response.statusText !== "OK"` (line 90) is an unreliable success check — `statusText` is not guaranteed to be the literal string `"OK"` across runtimes/proxies; use `response.ok` instead.

**`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`** — deviates from the codebase's own convention (`defaultHandler`/`defaultResponder`, used in `larkcalendar`, `office365calendar`, `hubspot` callbacks) for consistent error formatting/method handling. Concretely: no HTTP method check (a GET with a body would be processed), and `req.body` schema validation / `symmetricDecrypt` / `JSON.parse(keys)` are not wrapped in try/catch, so a malformed or tampered payload throws an uncaught error instead of a clean 4xx. Also, `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` silently falls back to an empty-string encryption key if the env var isn't configured, rather than failing fast with a clear configuration error — a self-hoster who forgets to set this key gets a confusing crypto error (or worse, weak/predictable behavior) instead of an obvious startup/config error.

**`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:56-93`** — find-then-create/update instead of an atomic upsert (acknowledged in the code's own comment: "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential"). Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appSlug)` can race and create duplicate credential rows. If the schema has (or can have) a unique constraint on `(userId, appId)`, an upsert keyed on that compound unique would remove the race; otherwise this should at least be documented as a known limitation.

**Testing** — no test files are included anywhere in this diff (`git diff --stat` shows only source files). This PR touches encryption/decryption of credentials, webhook auth, and OAuth token refresh across 8 provider integrations with zero automated coverage, which is a meaningful gap for security-sensitive, easy-to-silently-break logic (as demonstrated by findings #1–#3 above, none of which would be caught by a quick read).

**`packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:259`** — `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` is now dead logic: since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on parse failure, `tokenResponse.success` is always `true` by the time this line executes. Harmless but confusing; also the previous `console.error` diagnostic on parse failure was removed with no replacement (failures now throw with a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" and no context about which fields failed validation).

**`packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/api/add.ts:17`** — `WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`` was replaced with a hardcoded `"zoho-bigin"` string, discarding the existing single source of truth (`appConfig.slug`) for no apparent reason related to this PR's stated intent. Minor DRY regression.

**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/encodeOAuthState.ts` / `decodeOAuthState.ts`** — the two functions are structurally identical (parse `req.query.state` as JSON, then for "encode" immediately `JSON.stringify` it back). Naming implies `encodeOAuthState` should be building an outbound state parameter to attach to the auth-provider redirect URL, but it instead re-derives it from the *incoming* request's query string — likely pre-existing behavior carried over in the move, but worth a second look since it reads as dead/confusing code in a security-relevant OAuth path.

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication.rationale: The new webhook handler does a non-atomic read-then-write sequence: `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` followed by either `update` or `create`. This is a classic race window: two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appSlug/appId)` can both observe “no credential” and both attempt `create`. If there is no DB-level unique constraint, that can create duplicate rows; if there is a unique constraint, one request will fail (still a correctness/robustness issue). The diff itself clearly introduces this pattern and even notes the lack of upsert, so the finding is grounded in the shown code.
